Guide: Reaching steady state and calibrating

Source: vignettes/guide-calibrate-model.qmd

This guide gives an overview of the functions used to bring a mizer model to steady state and calibrate it to observed biomasses, yields and growth. For full documentation of each function, follow the links.

This covers the tune-to-data loop for an existing MizerParams object. To build the object from scratch first, see the guide to building a mizer model.

Every function here returns a new MizerParams — always reassign (params <- f(params, ...)). Change species parameters through species_params(params) <- ... so dependent quantities recalculate.

Finding the steady state

A freshly constructed model has only a rough spectrum. Settle it onto a steady state, which also sets the initial values used by calibration and by project():

params <- tuneSteadyState(params)
Function Use
tuneSteadyState(params) solve for the spectra with births and the resource held fixed, then adjust the parameters that generate them so those held values are steady too (the default choice while calibrating)
steadySingleSpecies(params) set each species to its single-species steady form, births held fixed, without changing the resource — a fast way to get a sensible starting spectrum before tuneSteadyState()
findSteadyState(params) change no parameter: births, resource and spectra settle together wherever the parameters you already have put them
projectUntilSettled(params) the same run as findSteadyState(params) but returning the MizerSim, when you want to watch the approach
isSteady(params) (experimental) TRUE if every required measure passes, FALSE if any fails, NA if coverage is incomplete without a demonstrated failure
getSteadyAssessment(params) (experimental) measures, tolerances, scope and missing support behind that verdict
getSteadyResidual(params) (experimental) each size class’s contribution to its species’ biomass drift, showing where it is not; rowSums() gives the per-species drift

The two finders differ in what they keep. tuneSteadyState() keeps the state — the birth rate and the resource abundance you supplied — and moves erepro/R_max and the resource capacity cc_pp to make it steady. findSteadyState() keeps every parameter and moves the state. During setup and calibration you almost always want tuneSteadyState(), or steadySingleSpecies() first: holding births constant lets the search settle reliably onto a steady state. Each process supplies a named default tuning strategy. Built-in Beverton-Holt and Ricker strategies preserve their law-specific reproduction_level. Use preserve for an explicitly supported alternative, such as "erepro" or "R_max" for Beverton-Holt, or select named strategies with strategies = c(reproduction = "preserve_erepro").

Extensions declare which states stay fixed, which evolve, and which parameters may be adjusted afterwards. A missing declaration is an error before the search, not permission to guess. joint selects registered strategies that own several coupled processes; those replace the corresponding local choices. Inspect getProcess(params) and getComponent(params, component)$definition for stored declarations. The current Newton solver can hold and later balance extension states, but cannot evolve arbitrary component states.

Balancing preserves the target state and all effective rates entering its equations, including final assembled recruitment. The independent checks also enforce declared parameter bounds and preserved quantities. A failure returns an error, without a generic optimisation fallback or a second steady-state search. The resulting off-target response, and hence stability, can still change.

balanceRDD(params) preserves the model’s current effective recruitment while adjusting its current reproduction law. Use rdd_target only when a separate calculation has established the intended constrained target; named partial targets leave other species’ recruitment and parameters alone when the strategy supports partial requests. matchGrowth(), matchBiomasses() and matchNumbers() retain the chosen law and balance only the selected species. setBevertonHolt() is instead an explicit switch to Beverton-Holt, preserving effective recruitment at the current state. Infeasible explicit controls are errors rather than silently adjusted values.

When not to use tuneSteadyState(). Holding births fixed is also its limit: every state it finds has the recruitment the model started with, and it gets there by changing erepro/R_max and cc_pp. So it is the wrong tool when

  • the question is where a model with given parameters settles, for instance under a changed fishing effort;
  • you are looking for more than one steady state: two alternative stable states found with it have different parameters, so they are not states of the same model;
  • a change in reproduction is the mechanism you are studying, as when predation thins a prey species and so raises its recruitment, or when a predator’s juveniles depend on the small prey that response produces (an emergent Allee effect).

Use findSteadyState(), or projectUntilSettled() to watch the approach, with the parameters fixed and starting from a suitable initial state, then findSteadyState(solver = "newton") to polish the result. A re-derived erepro greater than 1 is the sign that tuneSteadyState() was asked for a state that does not exist with births held where they were; see Diagnosing calibration problems.

Both take a solver argument. The default solver = "project" runs the dynamics until they settle. solver = "newton" (experimental, needs the nleqslv package) instead solves the steady-state equation directly, which converges even when the steady state is dynamically unstable, and discovers the support of the steady state automatically.

tuneSteadyState() returning is not proof that the model is steady. Its stopping test is the relative change in egg production over t_check, a proxy for the drift itself, and the run can also stop on a limit cycle, on a species going extinct, or simply at t_max. All four outcomes return a MizerParams object that looks the same. What distinguishes them is the "convergence" attribute, and the checks in Verifying the result:

params <- tuneSteadyState(params)
attr(params, "convergence")$attractor    # "fixed_point", "limit_cycle" or NA
attr(params, "convergence")$termination  # why the run stopped
attr(params, "convergence")$assessment   # measures, coverage and scope
attr(params, "convergence")$residual     # separate biomass-drift diagnostic
plot(getSteadyResidual(params))          # which species, and at which sizes

Read attractor together with assessment. A "fixed_point" requires all required assessments to pass. With scope = "conditional" that claim applies only with the named states fixed; the report retains those names. termination says how the run ended and converged whether the solver was happy. Neither alone establishes a whole-model steady state, and the legacy residual biomass number is no longer the verdict.

A termination of "residual_tolerance" is the ordinary success: the distance function dropped below distance_tol and every required assessment passed. "cycle_detected" means the search ran into a limit cycle — see the guide to analysing dynamic stability. "time_limit" means the run ran out of time: raise t_max, or get a better starting spectrum from steadySingleSpecies() first, and reach for solver = "newton" when the fixed point is dynamically unstable. "extinction" means a species is dying out, which is a modelling problem — see Diagnosing calibration problems. tuneSteadyState() says all of this in its messages too, but info_level = 0 suppresses those, so in a script the attribute is the reliable check.

A run that hits t_max having met distance_tol is worth recognising: the message names the drift as the reason, and it means the distance function went quiet while the model was still moving. Tightening distance_tol will not help; plot(getSteadyResidual(params)) shows what is actually moving.

The calibration loop

Do this only if you have observations. Observed biomasses live in the species-parameter column biomass_observed, optionally with a biomass_cutoff size threshold below which observations are not counted. Observed yields live in the gear-parameter column yield_observed, which gives the annual yield of each gear-species pair. The usual order:

params <- tuneSteadyState(params)    # 1. settle onto the steady state
params <- calibrateBiomass(params)   # 2. scale kappa so total modelled biomass
                                     #    matches total observed
params <- matchBiomasses(params)     # 3. adjust each species to its own observation
params <- matchGrowth(params)        # 4. rescale h, gamma, ks, k so each species
                                     #    reaches w_mat / w_inf on schedule
params <- tuneSteadyState(params)    # 5. re-converge after the changes

Re-run tuneSteadyState() after any match… step — those rescale each species separately, which is not a symmetry of the model, so whatever steady state it was on it is no longer on. They say so when they do it. The calibrate…() functions do not need it: they apply one overall scaling factor to the whole model, which is an exact symmetry and leaves the steady state untouched.

You do not have to remember this. getSteadyResidual() answers it, and summary(params) shows the verdict:

summary(params)                        # verdict, coverage and tolerance ratios
plot(getSteadyResidual(params))        # which species, and at which sizes
Function Adjusts To match Breaks steady state
calibrateBiomass() kappa (resource level) total community biomass no
matchBiomasses() per-species abundance each biomass_observed yes
matchGrowth() h, gamma, ks, k von Bertalanffy growth to w_mat/w_inf yes

matchGrowth() and matchBiomasses() pull on different parameters; alternate them, re-running tuneSteadyState() between, until both are satisfied — usually a few passes.

If your observations are numbers rather than weights, use calibrateNumber() and matchNumbers() in place of the two biomass functions. They are the same functions with the factor of the weight taken out of the size integral, and they read number_observed and number_cutoff instead of biomass_observed and biomass_cutoff. Mixing the two — matching some species on biomass and others on numbers — works, because each function ignores the species for which its own observation column is NA.

species_params(params)$number_observed <- c(Cod = 1e6, Herring = 4e8, ...)
params <- calibrateNumber(params)
params <- matchNumbers(params)
params <- tuneSteadyState(params)

Whichever pair you use, a <to>_cutoff value is the smallest size the observation counts, in grams: a survey that misses fish under 10 g is biomass_cutoff = 10, and the model is then integrated over the same range rather than over the whole spectrum. Leave it out and the whole size range is counted, which is the usual reason a model looks like it over-predicts a species by a wide margin.

Yields are not a calibration target in mizer itself: put the observed annual yield of each gear-species pair into the yield_observed column of gear_params() and compare it with the model using plotYieldObservedVsModel(), which sums the observations over the gears. Pass gear = a subset of the gear names to compare only their catch against only their observations. Use mizerExperimental::matchYield() to adjust the catchability so that the yields match. Yields depend on the fishing setup, so make sure gears and effort are right first — see the guide to setting up fishing.

Density-dependent reproduction

Set how strongly reproduction is density-limited. reproduction_level is the fraction of maximum recruitment realised at steady state (0 = density independent, closer to 1 = strongly limited):

reproduction_level(params) <- 0.25

Alternatively use setBevertonHolt() to specify R_max, erepro, or a per-species named vector. This does not change the steady state itself — it sets how the model responds to perturbations away from it. Read the current values back with reproduction_level(params), useful to check what a model was tuned to before changing it.

Verifying the result 

isSteady(params)                       # TRUE if settled within tolerance
summary(params)                        # still at the steady state?
attr(getSteadyResidual(params), "other")  # components, if the model has any
plotSpectra(params)                    # sensible, overlapping spectra?
plotGrowthCurves(params, species = "Cod")
plotBiomassObservedVsModel(params)     # points near the 1:1 line?
plotYieldObservedVsModel(params)

Whole-model coverage is the default. For built-in abundance states, the default measure integrates the magnitude of each size-class derivative, weighted by body mass. Each species and the resource is checked separately against atol + tol * integral(w * abs(N)), with atol = 1e-12 g/year and tol = 0.05 per year by default. The model’s size quadrature is respected. At zero abundance, zero change passes and positive inflow must fit the absolute tolerance. Taking magnitudes before summing prevents changes at different sizes from cancelling.

For the previous net-biomass criterion, explicitly request getSteadyAssessment(params, criterion = "biomass"). This can pass while the shape of a spectrum is changing, so it is a deliberate weaker criterion. Extension measures have their own units and tolerances; tol applies to the built-in measures. Use named tolerances overrides keyed by owner/measure to adjust an individual reported measure.

A component needs its own convergence capability even if it supplies an equation or a biomass measurement. Missing support appears in assessment$missing and assessment$unavailable; it cannot be treated as passing. Callback errors are errors. Solvers stop before starting if required support is missing.

Use scope = "conditional", fixed = "component:pool" to analyse a subsystem with a particular dynamic component held fixed. Other IDs are consumers and resource; several can be supplied together. The current solvers cannot hold consumers fixed, and Newton cannot evolve arbitrary extension states. A conditional result remains labelled conditional. A structurally prescribed input is recorded separately from a dynamic state fixed for this analysis.

When projection holds the size classes above a species’ retained support at zero, the drift diagnostic excludes inflow into those classes if they are empty. It still includes losses from the last retained class and inflow into empty classes inside the support. A small biomass drift indicates little net biomass change in the truncated model; it does not rule out changes within the size spectrum or establish that w_max is large enough for boundary losses to be negligible.

Populated classes above the support retain their algebraic drift, including mortality decay. If a projection clears that tail, the instantaneous removal is not represented by this finite diagnostic. The legacy upwind Euler path without diffusion can instead fill an empty tail; its diagnostic contributions are also retained. See the upper-boundary discussion in the numerical details for these limits.

project(params, check_steady = TRUE) makes the same check at the point where it matters, warning if the run is about to start from a state that is not a fixed point. It is off by default, because projecting a model away from its steady state is a normal thing to do.

When the model looks right, project it forward with the guide to running a mizer simulation and analyse the results with the guide to analysing and plotting mizer results.

Diagnosing calibration problems

  • tuneSteadyState() will not settle. The initial spectrum is probably far from the steady state. Run steadySingleSpecies(params) first to get a sensible starting spectrum, or take a smaller step in whatever parameter you changed and re-run. Persistent instability is a case for solver = "newton".
  • A species collapses to near-zero. Its mortality exceeds the growth it can fund. Check its predation-kernel parameters beta and sigma, its row of the interaction matrix, and whether its fishing mortality is too high. See the guide to understanding size-spectrum dynamics for the underlying physiological and trophic mechanics.
  • Biomass matches but growth is wrong (or vice versa). Alternate matchGrowth() and matchBiomasses(), re-running tuneSteadyState() between them.
  • tuneSteadyState() said it converged but the results still drift. Check attr(params, "convergence")$assessment, or summary(params), for which measures still fail, and reduce tuneSteadyState()’s distance_tol if it is too large. It warns when the two disagree.
  • tuneSteadyState() warns that a species requires “an unrealistic value greater than 1 for erepro”. The recruitment held during the search needs more eggs than that species’ spawners can produce in the state that was found, and the "convergence" attribute will not tell you so: it can still report a fixed point. Look at species_params(params)$erepro, because the warning reads the same for 1.01 as for 1e34. A value far above 1 means the state you asked for does not exist with births held at their current values, which is what happens when tuneSteadyState() is used to look for an alternative stable state or for a state that depends on a change in reproduction; use findSteadyState() or projectUntilSettled() with the parameters fixed instead (see Finding the steady state). A value just above 1 during calibration says the spawners cannot fund the recruitment they have: look at the species’ feeding level and growth before anything else.
  • Results move even though nothing was changed. The model was not at its steady state to begin with. plot(getSteadyResidual(params)) shows which species and which sizes are moving.

Interactive tuning

For hands-on tuning, the mizerExperimental package provides tuneParams(), a Shiny gadget that exposes sliders for the parameters above and re-runs tuneSteadyState() live. It is not part of core mizer — install and load mizerExperimental to use it.

Quick reference 

# ── Steady state ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
params <- tuneSteadyState(params)
params <- steadySingleSpecies(params)   # fast starting spectrum
params <- tuneSteadyState(params, solver = "newton")  # direct solve (experimental)

# ── Calibrate to data (re-run tuneSteadyState() after each) ───────────────────
params <- calibrateBiomass(params)      # total biomass  → kappa
params <- matchBiomasses(params)        # per-species biomass
params <- calibrateNumber(params)       # same, for `number_observed` instead
params <- matchNumbers(params)          #   of `biomass_observed`
params <- matchGrowth(params)           # growth → h, gamma, ks, k
params <- tuneSteadyState(params)       # re-converge

# ── Reproduction ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
reproduction_level(params) <- 0.25
reproduction_level(params)              # what the model is currently tuned to

# ── Verify ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
isSteady(params)                        # TRUE if settled within tolerance
summary(params)                         # includes the biomass-drift verdict
plot(getSteadyResidual(params))         # which species and sizes are still moving
plotSpectra(params)
plotGrowthCurves(params)
plotBiomassObservedVsModel(params)
plotYieldObservedVsModel(params)
